findings.why: The footnote says the visuals are AI illustrations standing in for results, so the ad shows skin outcomes nobody photographed, and a small-print disclaimer does not undo what the image shows (if the frames show clearer skin beside 'acne-prone', they also imply acne clearing, CLM-02). The rulebook rates CLM-15 as fix; my view is that this must not run until real evidence replaces the frames.
findings.fix: Replace the AI frames with real, consented, unretouched study photos carrying the study qualifier, or drop the result imagery and show the pack or texture instead; then rewrite or remove this footnote.

findings.span: Real, consented study photos are required before any use.
findings.why: This is an internal production instruction, not consumer copy, and it states outright that the creative is not cleared to run as built. Publishing it would print a team note on a paid ad and flag the visuals as placeholders.
findings.fix: Remove it from the creative, and resolve the imagery first (see the CLM-15 finding).

tone_read: The copy is on-voice: calm, led by the active and its strength, and it names the concern the clinical way ('oily, acne-prone skin') with no problem hook or hype. The visual is what clashes with the brand: AI-made 'results' under a 'Hide Nothing.' sign-off undercut the transparency that line promises.
language_read: Concentration is exact and on-format ('10% Niacinamide', matching Niacinamide 10% Face Serum), and the supporting actives (Matmarine, Zinc) are named precisely and appear on the product page. There are no efficacy verbs to hedge and no natural or chemical-free framing, and the ad rightly skips the page's 'clinically proven' and complexion claims.
